pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, 'making sense of a problem' means the child learns that a word problem describes a real situation to be understood before any number is touched. The proficient young solver restates what the story is asking in their own words, represents it with objects or a drawing, works toward an answer, and then checks whether that answer makes sense in the story. The single biggest teaching risk is the opposite habit: children being conditioned to grab the numbers and 'do a sum', a compulsion to calculate that suspends real-world sense-making. Teaching therefore centres on comprehension-first routines (retell the story, act it out with counters, ask 'what are we trying to find out?') rather than on cue-words or speed.
bestPractices: Comprehension first: have the child retell the problem in their own words and say what is being asked BEFORE any calculating
Represent the situation concretely — act it out with counters, fingers, or a simple drawing so the story structure (part-part-whole) is visible
Use numberless / progressively-revealed story problems so children reason about the relationship between quantities before a number invites them to compute
Model a short self-questioning routine aloud ('What is happening? What do I need to find? Does my answer make sense?') and have the child echo it
Deliberately pose the occasional unanswerable or 'silly' story so children learn that not every set of numbers yields a sum — sense-making is required
Never teach cue-word rules ('altogether means add'): build understanding of the situation, not word-to-operation mapping
keyRepresentations: Concrete objects / counters the child physically moves to enact the story
Part-part-whole picture (two groups combining into a whole)
Simple bar or strip drawing linking the known and unknown quantities
Numberless word-problem staging (reveal the story, then the question, then the numbers last)
A four-move frame: understand → represent → solve → check
commonMisconceptions: 'I look for the special word — altogether means add, left means take away' (keyword strategy, applied before the story is even read)
'Every problem is just a sum with the numbers in it' — computes an answer even for an unanswerable or nonsensical story (suspension of sense-making / compulsion to calculate)
Restating a salient number from the story instead of the quantity actually asked for
Treating being stuck as 'I can't do it' rather than a cue to represent the story a different way

learn.summary: For 5-6 year-olds, 'making sense of a problem' means treating a word problem as a real situation to understand before touching any number. Proficient young solvers restate what the story asks in their own words, represent it with objects or a drawing, work toward an answer, then check whether it makes sense in the story. The main teaching risk is the opposite habit — grabbing the numbers and 'doing a sum' (suspension of sense-making / compulsion to calculate). The core activity is a patient spoken 'thinking partner' routine that refuses a blurted number and builds comprehension first; concrete counters, numberless/progressively-revealed staging, a worked-example reveal, and a single reasonableness check are supporting approaches with different purposes.

activities.title: The thinking partner who won't take a number yet
feedback: When the child retells the story and names what is asked before computing, affirm that move explicitly: that understanding-first step is the goal.
If the child blurts a number, the partner does not accept it yet — it asks 'what is happening?' and 'how could you show that with your counters?'
When the child catches an unanswerable story ('that doesn't make sense, you can't work that out!'), the partner delights in the catch — this is the target moment.
Always close solvable stories with 'does your answer make sense in the story?' to plant the reasonableness habit.
activities.rationale: The topic is a dialogic habit: understanding the story and explaining a pathway before computing. A partner that poses a short story, asks self-questioning prompts, and refuses a bare number models the self-questioning routine; the occasional nonsensical story directly confronts the compulsion to calculate. Spoken or tapped responses keep turns short for this age. This is a proposed design, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process for students to monitor and reflect on their problem solving has strong evidence of improving achievement.

Students' primary difficulty with word problems is a 'suspension of sense-making' / 'compulsion to calculate' — they apply arithmetic to the numbers regardless of whether the result makes sense; numberless word problems and focusing on relationships before computing counter this.

Mathematically proficient students explain the meaning of a problem and look for entry points, and continually ask themselves 'Does this make sense?'; younger students rely on concrete objects or pictures to conceptualise and solve a problem.
learnerActions: Listen to a tiny within-10 spoken story from a friendly partner character, e.g. 'Three frogs were on a log and two more hopped on.'
Before giving any answer, retell the story in your own words and say what is being asked ('what are we trying to find out?').
Show the story with counters/frogs or fingers ('show me with your frogs') so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Work out an answer for a solvable story, then answer the partner's closing question: 'Does your answer make sense in the story?'
When the partner occasionally tells a deliberately silly story ('...so what colour is the pond?' or '...so how old is the cat?'), catch that it cannot be worked out and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A word problem is a situation to understand, not just numbers to do a sum with; sense-making and a reasonableness check come before and after calculating.

activities.title: Numberless, progressively-revealed story with a part-whole workspace
feedback: The 'does this match the story?' prompt checks the child's model against the situation rather than only the final number.
If the model doesn't match the story, invite the child to re-place counters to show the two parts and the whole.
activities.rationale: Staging the reveal (picture, then question, then numbers) and giving a part-whole mat with draggable counters lets the child build a representation before a number invites computing, countering the compulsion to calculate and building the visual-representation skill. The dragging and part-whole mat are concrete interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Students' primary difficulty with word problems is a 'suspension of sense-making' / 'compulsion to calculate' — they apply arithmetic to the numbers regardless of whether the result makes sense; numberless word problems and focusing on relationships before computing counter this.

Mathematically proficient students explain the meaning of a problem and look for entry points, and continually ask themselves 'Does this make sense?'; younger students rely on concrete objects or pictures to conceptualise and solve a problem.
learnerActions: See the story picture first, then the question, with the numbers revealed last.
With a workspace of draggable counters and a part-whole mat, place objects to model the situation and the relationship between the quantities.
Only after modelling, use the number pad that appears to find the answer.
Respond to a 'does this match the story?' check that compares your model to the situation, not just the final number.
activities.intendedInsight: Children reason about the relationship between quantities before a number invites them to compute, building a visual representation of the situation.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal worked example of the four moves
feedback: Prompt the child to say which phase comes next before revealing it, so they anticipate the routine rather than only watching.
activities.rationale: A worked-example reveal makes the four-move routine explicit and models the self-questioning a solver uses. Used as a companion to the doing-centred activities: it shows the sense-making rather than requiring the child to perform it, so it supports but does not replace practising the habit.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process for students to monitor and reflect on their problem solving has strong evidence of improving achievement.
learnerActions: Work through one story where each phase can be revealed: understand → represent → solve → check.
At each phase, see what a good solver asks themselves ('What is happening? What do I need to find? Does my answer make sense?').
Echo the self-questioning routine aloud after seeing it modelled.
activities.intendedInsight: The understand/represent/solve/check routine becomes visible as a sequence a solver actually follows.

activities.title: Single reasonableness check (which answer could not be right?)
feedback: Accept justifications grounded in the story ('she gave some away so it must be fewer'); gently redirect answers that only restate a computation.
If the child says 'more' is possible after giving away, re-enact with counters to show that, when she only gives stickers away and gets none, the number she has can only go down.
activities.rationale: A single reasonableness item keeps the focus on sense-checking rather than producing answers fast. This is deliberately restricted to reasonableness: a battery of scored sums would reward speed and reinforce the compulsion to calculate this topic must dislodge.
sourceClaims: Students' primary difficulty with word problems is a 'suspension of sense-making' / 'compulsion to calculate' — they apply arithmetic to the numbers regardless of whether the result makes sense; numberless word problems and focusing on relationships before computing counter this.
learnerActions: Given a within-10 story and a candidate answer, decide whether the answer could be right and explain why or why not.
For example: 'Maya has 6 stickers and gives some away. Could she end up with MORE than 6 stickers? How do you know?'
Explain using the situation ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'), not by re-doing the sum.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasonableness is judged by the situation, so an answer can be ruled out before or without recomputing.

constraints: Comprehension first: have the child retell the problem in their own words and say what is being asked BEFORE any calculating.

Never teach cue-word rules ('altogether means add', 'left means take away'); build understanding of the situation, not word-to-operation mapping. Cue words misfire when the word points the wrong way — e.g. a 'more' comparison story whose answer is actually found by subtracting.
Represent the situation concretely (counters, fingers, a simple drawing, or a simple bar/strip drawing linking the known and unknown quantities) so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Deliberately include the occasional unanswerable or 'silly' story so children learn not every set of numbers yields a sum; keep most stories genuinely solvable.
The tap-to-reveal worked example shows the routine but has the child watch rather than do it; use it as a companion, not the main practice for a habit that must be practised.

Scored, speed-oriented quizzing of multiple sums is unsuitable here: it can score the final number but not 'made sense of the story', and it reinforces the compulsion to calculate. A single reasonableness item is acceptable; a battery of sums is not.

Making sense of a word problem is a comprehension task, not a spatial one; a 3-D handling environment is not recommended for this topic because it adds handling cost without serving the comprehension-first goal. This is a scoped suitability judgement, not a claim that 3-D adds nothing in general.
When a child is stuck, scaffold by offering a representation ('let's put out the counters') and naming the move ('when it's tricky, we show it a different way'), rather than reteaching the concept.
Watch for restating a salient number from the story instead of the quantity actually asked for.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles, not these specific activities' effectiveness.

The legacy claims that a scored quiz 'cannot' teach this and that 3-D 'adds nothing' have been softened to scoped suitability notes with stated affordances/limits; the cited sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity between artefact types.

Source claims are copied exactly and attached only where they directly support the stated rationale; the WWC self-questioning evidence is for grades 4-8, while this topic targets ages 5-6, so transfer of that evidence to this age band is an assumption, not a verified finding.
The non-answerable 'silly story' device is a legitimate sense-making probe but should be used sparingly so children do not learn to distrust all stories; keep most stories genuinely solvable.

probeDeeper: 'Tell me the story again without saying any numbers — what is happening?' (checks a situation model, not word-matching)
'Show me with your counters why the answer is 4.' (pushes the assertion into a because-of-the-situation justification)
Counterexample: 'Here's another one — there are 5 red apples and 3 green apples, how old is the girl?' A sense-maker notices it can't be worked out; a number-grabber answers 8.
'Could Maya end up with MORE than 6 stickers after giving some away? How do you know?' (reasonableness by the situation)
assess.correctAnswer: There is no single scored answer — listen for a child who first makes sense of the situation: retells the story in their own words, names what is being asked (how many Maya has left), represents it (moves 6 counters and takes 2 away, or draws), gives 4, and can say why 4 makes sense (she started with 6 and lost some, so it must be fewer than 6). The disposition, not the arithmetic, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate with no real-world check: 'every problem is a sum you do with the numbers' — the child computes and stops, and will produce a number even for a story that can't be answered.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use numberless / progressively-revealed stories and occasional unanswerable ones; make 'does this make sense in real life?' a routine closing question. Confront the specific case: 'could we really know her age from the apples?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When told a nonsensical story ('5 red apples and 3 green apples — how old is the girl?'), the child confidently gives a number (usually 8) rather than saying it can't be worked out.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword operation-mapping: picks the operation from a cue word ('altogether' = add, 'gave away' = subtract) before reading or understanding the whole story.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Never use keyword posters; have the child retell the story and model it with objects so the structure, not the word, drives the choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names an operation from one word and misfires when the word points the wrong way (e.g. a 'more' comparison story where the answer is found by subtracting).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats being stuck as 'I can't do it' and abandons, rather than trying to represent the story another way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach the concept: offer a representation ('let's put out the counters') and name the move — 'when it's tricky, we show it a different way'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child stops and says 'I don't get it' without attempting to act it out or draw; has the general persistence habit but doesn't yet apply it in maths.

responseLevels.gap: Jumps to a number without engaging the story; grabs the numbers and applies an operation; answers the nonsensical apples problem with a number and cannot say what is being asked.
responseLevels.full: Leads with the situation: retells the problem, represents it, and justifies the answer BY the story ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'); spontaneously flags the unanswerable problem as making no sense, and transfers this to a new story unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can restate the story and often gets the right number, but treats making-sense and checking as separate add-ons — recites 'understand, then check' or represents when prompted, yet does not spontaneously use the situation to justify or sense-check the answer.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read the child a short within-10 story, e.g. 'Maya had 6 stickers. She gave 2 to her friend.' Then, before asking for any answer, ask: 'What is this story about — can you tell it back to me in your own words? What are we trying to find out? Show me how you'd work it out.' Finish with: 'How would you know if your answer makes sense?' Treat it as a discussion, not a test — you are surfacing how the child thinks about problems, not marking a number right or wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who is genuinely making sense pauses on the STORY first — retells it, shows it, and can justify the answer by the situation ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'). A child in the compulsion-to-calculate habit skips straight to a number and, tellingly, will still produce a number for a nonsensical story and cannot say why it makes sense. The gap shows in the reasoning and the sense-check, not in whether they can subtract.

sources.claim: The keyword strategy has students tie a single word to an operation without understanding the whole text; it superficially focuses on certain words rather than the problem's structure and should be replaced by schema (structure) instruction.
